title: Wrongosaurus: a paleontology game where the dinosaurs you build don't have to be right
author: Kreed22vR
selftext:
Hi all. I joined recently and I've loved seeing what everyone here is making. It's pushed me to finally share mine.

This is Wrongosaurus (working title). I used to love Spore, mostly for the creature creator, and I'm a huge dinosaur and paleontology fan. I always wanted to mix the two. So: you're a paleontologist, you dig up fossils, and then you build whatever creature you want from the bones. It doesn't have to be accurate. That's the point.

It's my first game and I'm not a coder. My background is animation and graphic design. I direct and Claude Code does the building, in Godot, with Blender for the 3D models.

The trailer shows an early build. I'm already reworking how the digs work and look, and how the world looks, so it's rough in places. Many placeholder models and animations for now.

The thing I'm stuck on: digging is the core of the game and you do it over and over, and I can feel it turning into a chore. If you've built a game around one repeated action, what kept it fun?

Any other thoughts are welcome too. Thanks, and keep making cool games.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
'The thing I'm stuck on: digging is the core of the game and you do it over and over, and I can feel it turning into a chore. If you've built a game around one repeated action, what kept it fun?'

A key thing to understand is that most games have one core loop. Having one action you expect the player to repeat is totally normal and fine.

The thing to get right is balancing that loop. Players go dig -> then they \[X\] -> then they \[Y\] -> then they \[Z\] -> then they go back to digging. Please note that you don't need like 4-5 things or whatever for the loop, a lot of games have only two core components to the loop and that's perfectly fine.

A lot of designs (including my own) balance that loop of play by having each system serve as fuel for the next system. XCOM and XCOM 2 do this very beautifully: you go on mission to get resources, you spend those resource at your base to get more kit, you bring that kit onto missions. Missions gas-up what you can do at the base, the base gasses-up what you can bring on missions.

Darkest Dungeon 1 has a similar approach.

Tears of the Kingdom has an elegant and more complex loop; I'd recommend looking up some videos on YouTube that explore it's system brilliance in depth. 

For your game, getting this balance right means the digging, or any other component of the game, never really becomes monotonous or feels grindy because doing it requires fuel that the player depletes and then they go do a different activity to get more fuel. This inherently create micro-goals for the player, and if you want you can further enhance those micro-goals by recognizing them in playtesting and then setting-up UI elements and/or rewards systems that give feedback on achieving micro-goals. Collect a Pokemon, it goes into the Pokedex. That kind of thing.

comments.author: Material-Database-24
comments.body:
So nice to see such novel idea here. Your working tittle got a chuckle out of me, keep it!

I think there two possible directions from which to choose:
1) is this a casual fun game or
2) is this something that suppose to addict, frustrate and reward

If 1) is the case, forget the "game" aspects. Just give the tools, make the bones abdutant. And maybe add some fun final touch, like 3 test scenarios which will test how the wrongosaurus would have survived - walking rough lands, drinking water, ???.

If as 2), then you need progress elements -like new better tools the further you play, harder to find bones, some element that causes bones to get destroyed, etc.

I personally would suggest just 1). Keep it casual and fun, not too much gaming elements. Something where one wrongosaurus build takes max ~15min.

Or if you do 2) give players a "random bones casual mode" where player gets randomly picked bones directly to build their wrongosaurus.

In both cases, you could add "multiplayer" element via shared gallery, where people can show their wrongosauruses.

comments.author: cdcox
comments.body:
Fantastic looking game.

Some random ideas as to how to make a core fun. 

1. Add on abilities and skills. Show big/rare skeletons the player can get to yet, give them to tools to build up to it. Bigger hits, faster digging, more precision for little bones, automatic tools for certain repeated tasks. Divergent trees that require or allow clever solutions are the best. 

2. Make the digging skilled but not repetitious. For example better hits get you bigger skeletons. Tighter cuts have less cleaning etc. Give the players something to work for instead of just wariowaring it. Give the player room for skill expression. This is what most sim games do, lots of repetition and only a few tools but when you nail a skill flawlessly and fast you feel amazing.

3. Emergent elements. Cost/benefit. If you have multiple bones stacked which one do you go for. Are there better fossils? Real fossils come in messy piles. Finding the right tool to cut into a messy pile and having room to lose is great. Have tools with overlapping responsibilities. Do you pull a big chunk out or go for a quick small one. Elements that might make you make timed decisions, rain, hole collapse, work day, sand storms. These are things that affect real digs. 

4. Include the dinosaurs somehow (if you want to go full factory game with it with it). It links the build phase with the work phase. Maybe you need a ground dude because you want to tear into things, or something big and strong to drag stuff. This is by far the hardest and is kind of a different less casual game but am spitballing here. 

5. Bring in a secondary loop. Maybe you have a zoo or something and people make requests of certain things so you are hunting for the right kinds of fossils in a given day. Gives the players goals and objectives that can make succeeding at a simple task feel amazing. Works best if monetary rewards unlock new tools. This is also how a lot of simulation games play out.

What it really plays into is: what kind of game are you making? A light simulation game (like electrican simulator)? A heavy simulation game? A factory game? A whacky physicsy game? A numbers go up game? What do you love doing when you play it over and over? What is boring or laggy? What parts do you dread to test because they suck. Lean into the fun parts and give people the ability to mitigate the boring parts and optimize the core loop until it feels snappy and fun. Try weird things like making everything way faster or way slower or stacking tons of things on top of each other etc. AI allows so much experimentation.

replies.author: Kreed22vR
replies.body:
Thank you so much for this, there's a lot here and I've read it a few times now! Quite a bit of it lines up with where I'm heading:   
  
Tools you build up to: yes. New tools will arrive as you reach digs that need them, and I like the idea of showing a big skeleton you can't get to yet.   
  
Skilled digging: definitely. I want careful work to pay off, so a clean dig gives you a bone in better condition, and each tool should feel different to use.   
  
Including the dinosaurs: this is the one I'm most excited about. Creatures you build will help at the digs, and some digs will need a creature built a certain way. (digs in high-up places require you to make a dino with a super long neck, or long legs etc.)  
  
A secondary loop: yes, you'll run a museum, and the money it brings in goes back into better tools. Requests for certain fossils is a cool idea on top of that.

I'm keeping it on the chill side, so probably no storms or timers, but digging into a messy pile of bones and choosing what to go for is a cool idea.

I think it's a light, relaxed sim. Really appreciate you taking the time, this helped a lot!

Have you played fossil fighters?

They have a fossil cleaning process that takes up a bunch of time- about a third of the game alongside fighting and digging up the fossils in the first place.

They’ve got special fossil types like gems that are easy to clean and dark fossils which need a hammer to break the outer shell- but hammer can break things. You get upgrades to your tools and can even have a buddy clean them for you if you don’t want to- but they will be far from perfect cleans (and you can upgrade his skills too). Second game introduced wondrous and mythic fossils that gave your Dino’s special effects 

Ultimately it acted as progression for a collection system so I think some things are allowed to feel like chores so long as the payoff is exciting
